newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel official warns against rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel official warns against rate cuts.

text.p: The head of the Bank of Israel's monetary department has warned against lowering interest rates before inflation is within a seven to 10 percent target range for 1997.

David Klein, in an internal paper published in the daily newspaper Haaretz on Wednesday, said the central bank must not miss another opportunity to bring inflation down to the levels of Western industrialised countries.
He said the Bank of Israel acted hastily in lowering interest rates in mid-1993 and mid-1995 after relatively low monthly consumer price indices, missing a chance to tame long-term inflation.
"We still have an opportunity to avoid re-playing this scenario in which interest rates are lowered before inflation has stabilised within the target range," Klein wrote.
Despite the appearance of a slowdown in inflation in the last few months, the figure is still relatively high compared to Western levels, he said.

The Bank of Israel's base interest rate peaked in mid-year at 17 percent but has since fallen to 14.7 percent. Consumer prices were running at a 14.6 percent annual rate in first-half 1996, slowing to half that in the second to a full-year figure of 10.6 percent.
For 1997, the inflation target is seven to 10 percent.
Last week, Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said significant interest rate cuts would not come until he saw that budget cuts were being successfully implemented.

In his paper, Klein wrote: "Regretfully, every additional month of 1996 saw new records being set for the government deficit and in December alone, the deficit was more than half the planned total for the whole year," Klein wrote.

The government's 1996 deficit ballooned to 4.7 percent of gross domestic product. The 1997 budget calls for spending cuts, new taxes and other revenue-raising measures designed to keep the deficit to 2.8 percent.
"The very big (Budget) deviation in 1996, which came after another big deviation in 1995, is already a heavy mortgage for 1997," Klein said.
